changes.before: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and removes only the first node or two that drain a tumour, sparing patients the arm swelling (lymphoedema) that removing all nodes causes. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

after: A node's capsule surrounds adjoining cortical, paracortical and medullary regions, with B-cell follicles and T-cell regions. These are adjoining tissue regions rather than sealed rooms. Afferent lymph enters the subcapsular sinus near the outer surface and passes toward medullary sinuses and an efferent vessel at the hilum. Efferent lymph can carry cells as well as fluid onward through lymphatics. Its eventual return to venous blood is downstream, rather than a direct junction to the vein shown beside a node in a simplified drawing.

One simplified route for blood is artery, capillary network, high endothelial venule (HEV), then venous outlet; Brulois and colleagues traced these connections in mouse peripheral nodes. Naive lymphocytes can cross from HEV blood into node tissue. In a diagram, keep that cell movement distinct from blood flow and lymph flow; red cells stay in the blood compartment. Label and enlargement leaders do not show transport or specify a unique crossing mechanism or timing. Nor does one illustrated route map every vessel, dictate every cell's path or demonstrate priming.

Imaging, drainage mapping, sampled-tissue pathology and controlled immune-response experiments answer different questions. Record the node, tissue region, collection method and time. In a fictional earlier-antigen example, arrival before migrating dendritic cells is possible, but uptake, presentation and antigen-dependent activation still need their own measurements. Neither arrival nor node size diagnoses cancer involvement or useful priming.

changes.before: The body's response to injury or infection: immune cells and fluid rush in, causing redness, heat and swelling. Short bursts heal; long-term smouldering inflammation promotes cancer.
changes.after: Inflammation is a tissue response to infection, injury or tissue stress. It can support repair or contribute to harm; the cause, location and duration matter.
changes.reason: Remove deterministic short-response/healing and chronic-response/cancer framing. Medzhitov and Ortega-Gomez complete review abstracts plus contextual primary mechanisms support a conditional definition.

changes.before: Chronic inflammation from infection (hepatitis B and C, H. pylori, HPV), irritation (tobacco, asbestos, acid reflux) or disease (ulcerative colitis) supplies growth factors, free radicals that mutate DNA, and blood-vessel growth, and it is estimated to underlie around a fifth of cancers; 'tumour-promoting inflammation' is a recognised enabling characteristic in the hallmarks of cancer. Yet inflammation is also how the immune system attacks tumours, and an 'inflamed' or 'hot' tumour is one full of T cells that responds well to checkpoint inhibitors. Aspirin and other anti-inflammatory drugs reduce colorectal cancer risk, and the inflammatory markers CRP and IL-6 track cachexia and prognosis. Inflammation is not the same as infection: infection and injury are classic triggers, and tissue stress or malfunction can induce a graded response, called para-inflammation, that relies mainly on tissue-resident macrophages (Medzhitov, 2008). Recruited cells can support containment and repair, or persist and add to injury, and increased vessel permeability is not the growth of new vessels. Resolution is a coordinated and active process that restores tissue integrity and function, and is not simply everything switching off (Ortega-Gómez et al., 2013). In experimental cancer systems one DNA-sensing pathway has had opposite roles: host STING-dependent sensing was needed for spontaneous CD8 T-cell priming against mouse tumours (Woo et al., 2014), while a tumour-cell response to cytosolic DNA in chromosomally unstable tumours promoted metastasis (Bakhoum et al., 2018). These are contextual mechanisms and not a head-to-head clinical comparison. Inflammation after an intervention does not show tumour-specific immune learning: a local reaction, immunogenic cell death, recognition of untreated cancer cells and clinical benefit each need their own evidence, and one raised blood marker does not identify the source of inflammation. Acute against chronic and local against systemic are separate axes, and they need not share a trigger or a consequence.

after: Sterile inflammation means an inflammatory response without an initiating infection; tissue injury can provide such a context. A short response is not guaranteed to heal, and persistent signalling does not establish one inevitable outcome. Acute versus chronic describes time, while local versus systemic describes distribution.

Locate tissue signals, the blood-vessel lumen and recruited cells separately. A cell crossing the vessel wall and fluid or proteins entering tissue are different movements, neither a new vessel growing. Swelling, a cytokine concentration, a fraction of marker-positive cells and a mixed-tissue RNA programme also have different units and denominators. State the specimen, time and quantity; a bulk programme does not identify every producing cell. In the fictional swelling-plus-RNA example, no antigen-specific response or target-cell killing was tested. That observation alone identifies neither the cause nor useful tumour immunity.
changes.reason: Add connected physiology and measurement-reading paragraphs. Sterile injury and varied outcomes have review scope; compartment/denominator and fictional-case limits are premise-backed reading rules, not new clinical tests.

changes.before: CD163 is a scavenger receptor for haemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes and is confined to monocytes and macrophages. It is the marker most often used to identify alternatively activated macrophages, the phenotype associated with tissue repair and immune suppression rather than with killing, and so it is the standard stain for counting tumour-associated macrophages in a tissue section. A soluble form shed into blood is measured in inflammatory disease. CD163 is the practical link between the macrophage record on this site and the agents aimed at that compartment, such as the CSF1R antibodies.
changes.after: CD163 is a receptor expressed by monocytes and mature macrophages. It helps clear haemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes. UniProt also describes a soluble form shed from the cell surface that may be used to monitor macrophage activation in inflammatory conditions. In a tumour sample, CD163 staining identifies cells expressing the receptor. The macrophage-activation consensus recommends describing the cells, their activating conditions and a collection of markers, rather than reducing activation to two fixed M1 and M2 types. The reading rule is to interpret CD163 with the other markers, tissue location and assay conditions; one marker alone does not establish tumour-supporting function or predict benefit from a drug aimed at the macrophage compartment.
